In linear algebra, '''operator monotone functions''' are an important type of [[real-valued function]], fully classified by [[Charles Löwner]] in 1934.{{r|low}} They are closely related to operator concave and operator convex functions, and are encountered in [[operator theory]] and in [[matrix theory]], and led to the [[Löwner–Heinz inequality]].{{r|eom}}{{r|pat}} Operator monotone functions are called in other contexts complete Bernstein function, [[Nevanlinna function]], Pick function or class (S) function.{{r|SSV}}

==Definition==
{{See also|Trace inequality#Operator monotone}}

A function <math>f : I \to \Reals</math> defined on an interval <math>I \subseteq \Reals</math> is said to be '''operator monotone''' if whenever <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are [[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian matrices]] (of any size/dimensions) whose [[eigenvalues and eigenvectors|eigenvalue]]s all belong to the domain of <math>f</math> and whose difference <math>A - B</math> is a [[positive semi-definite matrix]], then necessarily <math>f(A) - f(B) \geq 0</math> where <math>f(A)</math> and <math>f(B)</math> are the values of the [[matrix function]] [[matrix function#Extending scalar function to matrix functions|induced by <math>f</math>]] (which are matrices of the same size as <math>A</math> and <math>B</math>).  The function <math>f</math> is said to be n-matrix monotone (or just n-monotone) if the above holds for any matrices <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> of size <math>n</math> (but not necessarily of other sizes).

'''Notation'''

This definition is frequently expressed with the notation that is now defined. 

Write <math>A \geq 0</math> to indicate that a matrix <math>A</math> is [[Positive semi-definite matrix|positive semi-definite]] and write <math>A \geq B</math> to indicate that the difference <math>A - B</math> of two matrices <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> satisfies <math>A - B \geq 0</math> (that is, <math>A - B</math> is positive semi-definite). 

With <math>f : I \to \Reals</math> and <math>A</math> as in the theorem's statement, the value of the [[matrix function]] <math>f(A)</math> is the matrix (of the same size as <math>A</math>) [[Analytic function of a matrix#Hermitian matrices|defined in terms of]] its <math>A</math>'s [[Spectral theorem|spectral decomposition]] <math>A = \sum_j \lambda_j P_j</math> by
<math display="block">f(A) = \sum_j f(\lambda_j)P_j ~,</math> 
where the <math>\lambda_j</math> are the eigenvalues of <math>A</math> with corresponding [[Projection (linear algebra)|projectors]] <math>P_j.</math> 

The definition of an operator monotone function may now be restated as:

A function <math>f : I \to \Reals</math> defined on an interval <math>I \subseteq \Reals</math> said to be ''operator monotone'' if (and only if) for all positive integers <math>n,</math> and all <math>n \times n</math> [[Hermitian matrix|Hermitian matrices]] <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> with eigenvalues in <math>I,</math> if <math>A \geq B</math> then <math>f(A) \geq f(B).</math>

==Löwner’s theorem on holomorphic extension==

[[Charles Löwner|Löwner]]’s theorem{{r|low}} states that a function <math>f</math> is operator monotone if and only if it allows an [[analytic continuation]] to the [[upper half-plane]] with non-negative imaginary part.

More generally, a function <math>f(z) \geq 0</math> for <math>z \geq 0</math> is operator monotone if and only if it extends to a [[Holomorphic function|holomorphic]] function on <math>\C \setminus (-\infty, 0]</math> such that
:<math> \begin{align} \operatorname{Im} f(z) & \ge 0 \qquad && \text{if } \operatorname{Im} z \ge 0 , \\
\operatorname{Im} f(z) & \le 0 \qquad && \text{if } \operatorname{Im} z \le 0 . \end{align} </math>
which can be summarized as <math>\operatorname{Im} f(z) \operatorname{Im} z \ge 0</math>.

== Relation to Bernstein functions ==
Operator monotone functions are a special type of Bernstein function.  If we write the Bernstein representation of the Bernstein function <math>f</math> as<math display="block">f(t) = a + bt + \int_0^\infty \left(1 - e^{-tx}\right) \mu(dx),</math>then <math>f</math> is operator monotone if and only if the measure <math>\mu</math> has a density function and this function is completely monotone, which explains why such a function <math>f</math> is also called a complete Bernstein function.
